Gerald Stanley Lee published The Ghost in the White House in 1920, as America chose a new president. Lee, a popular writer on crowds and genius, offers suggestions for a President whom everyone can work with. He presents a programme and a sketch of what the next President will be like as a fellow human being. Name, eyes, and party he leaves for others to fill in later.

The ghost of the title is the public's own imagined President, haunting the real one. Lee asks how a whole people can express what they want and actually get it. His style is breezy, paradoxical, and hopeful. The book is a period piece of post-war idealism about democracy.

podcast-dannyjones--FQghS0GRhU:
Science writer Nadia Drake joins host Danny Jones for a long conversation that ranges well past her usual beat. Drake has covered space for major outlets. Here she fields questions about moon bases and odd features reported on Mars. She also takes up the uncontacted tribes of the Amazon, who still live apart from the modern world.

Jones steers the talk toward what officials might not be saying, and Drake answers as a working investigator would, weighing claims against evidence. The mix is the appeal: one guest moving from lunar plans to jungle peoples in a single sitting. Listeners should treat the wilder claims as the speakers' own, offered in a podcast built for speculation as much as for reporting.

Comedian Matt Rife joins Joe Rogan to tell of his ghost hunt in the Conjuring House in a segment from the show. The house is the Rhode Island farm tied to the Perron family case and the hit horror film. Rife is a young comic with a huge online crowd.

Rife tells what his night in the house felt like, from the cold rooms to the sounds he could not place. He shares why he bought rights in the place, as he tells it. Rogan asks if he is now a true believer. Listeners get a fun, spooky tale. The library holds the segment as an archive record.

Back in episode 371 of the Joe Rogan Experience, Rick Doblin made an early version of the case he is still making today. Doblin founded the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies to turn banned drugs into legal medicines. At this point, that goal was still distant.

He explains the first trial results for MDMA as a treatment for PTSD and why he thought regulators could be won over. Rogan, new to the subject then, asks basic questions that keep the talk clear. Heard now, the episode is a time capsule: the starting line of a campaign that later reached the edge of approval.
